{{Short description|Line vortex}}
In [[fluid dynamics]], the '''Lamb–Oseen vortex''' models a line [[vortex]] that decays due to [[viscosity]]. This vortex is named after [[Horace Lamb]] and  [[Carl Wilhelm Oseen]].<ref>Oseen, C. W. (1912). Uber die Wirbelbewegung in einer reibenden Flussigkeit. Ark. Mat. Astro. Fys., 7, 14–26.</ref><ref>{{Cite book |author1=Saffman, P. G. |author2=Ablowitz, Mark J. |author3=J. Hinch, E. |author4=Ockendon, J. R. |author5=Olver, Peter J. |author5-link=Peter J. Olver | title=Vortex dynamics | year=1992 | publisher=Cambridge University Press | location=Cambridge  | isbn=0-521-47739-5 }} p. 253.</ref>

[[File:Lamb-Oseen vortex.svg|right|thumb|Vector plot of the Lamb–Oseen vortex velocity field.]]

[[File:Lamb–Oseen vortex animation.gif|thumb|Evolution of a Lamb–Oseen vortex in air in real time. Free-floating test particles reveal the velocity and vorticity pattern. (scale: image is 20 cm wide)]]

== Mathematical description ==
[[Carl Wilhelm Oseen|Oseen]] looked for a solution for the [[Navier–Stokes equations]] in cylindrical coordinates <math>(r,\theta,z)</math> with velocity components <math>(v_r,v_\theta,v_z)</math> of the form
: <math>v_r=0, \quad v_\theta=\frac{\Gamma}{2\pi r}g(r,t), \quad v_z=0.</math>
where <math>\Gamma</math> is the [[Circulation (fluid dynamics)|circulation]] of the vortex core. Navier–Stokes equations lead to
: <math>\frac{\partial g}{\partial t} = \nu\left(\frac{\partial^2 g}{\partial r^2} - \frac{1}{r} \frac{\partial g}{\partial r}\right)</math>
which, subject to the conditions that it is regular at <math>r=0</math> and becomes unity as {{tmath| r\rightarrow\infty }}, leads to <ref name="DrazinRiley">{{cite book |last1=Drazin |first1=Philip |last2=Riley |first2=Norman |title=The Navier-Stokes Equations: A Classification of Flows and Exact Solutions (No. 334). |date=2006 |publisher=Cambridge University Press  |isbn=9780521681629 |pages=8, 169-172 |url=https://books.google.com/books/about/The_Navier_Stokes_Equations.html?id=9SHzrFhVO30C |access-date=27 June 2026 |language=en}}</ref>
: <math>g(r,t) = 1-\mathrm{e}^{-r^2/4\nu t},</math>
where <math>\nu</math> is the [[kinematic viscosity]] of the fluid. At {{tmath|1= t=0 }}, we have a potential vortex (free or irrotational vortex) with concentrated [[vorticity]] at the <math>z</math>-axis; and this vorticity diffuses away as time  passes.

The only non-zero vorticity component is in the <math>z</math>-direction, given by
: <math>\omega_z(r,t) = \frac{\Gamma}{4\pi \nu t} \mathrm{e}^{-r^2/4\nu t}.</math>

The [[pressure]] field simply ensures the vortex rotates in the [[circumference|circumferential]] direction, providing the [[centripetal]] force
: <math> {\partial p \over \partial r} = \rho {v^2 \over r},</math>
where <math>\rho</math> is the constant density.<ref>{{cite book | author=G.K. Batchelor |author-link=George Batchelor | year=1967 | title= An Introduction to Fluid Dynamics |publisher=Cambridge University Press }}</ref> Below are two methods by which Oseen's vortex can be derived.

{{math proof|title=Derivation of the Lamb-Oseen vortex in polar coordinates |proof=

We begin with the polar coordinate <math>(r,\theta)\in \mathbb{R}^2 </math> vector field, <math>\vec{v}=\left( 0, v_{\theta} \right)</math> in which the azimuthal momentum equation reduces to the advectionless form,<ref name="DrazinRiley" />
<math display="block"> \frac{\partial v_\theta}{\partial t} = \nu \left(\frac{\partial^2 v_\theta}{\partial r^2}+\frac{1}{r}\frac{\partial v_\theta}{\partial r} -\frac{v_\theta}{r^2}\right) </math>
which is subject to the following boundary conditions:
<math display="block"> \begin{Bmatrix} v_{\theta} (0,t)= 0  ,& v_{\theta}(r\to \infty ,t)=0 \\ v_{\theta}(r,0)=\frac{\Gamma}{2\pi r} ,&  v_{\theta}(r,t\to \infty)=0 \end{Bmatrix}</math>
By the substitution, <math> v_\theta (r,t)=\frac{\Gamma}{2\pi r}g(r,t)</math>, given some unknown <math>g : \mathbb{R}^2 \to \mathbb{R}^2 </math>, we have,

<math display="block"> 
\begin{align}
    \frac{\partial v_\theta}{\partial t}&=\nu \left(\frac{\partial^2 v_\theta}{\partial r^2}+\frac{1}{r}\frac{\partial v_\theta}{\partial r} -\frac{v_\theta}{r^2}\right)\\
    \iff\  \frac{\partial}{\partial t}\left( \frac{\Gamma}{2\pi r}g(r,t)\right) &=\nu \left(\frac{\partial^2}{\partial r^2}\left( \frac{\Gamma}{2\pi r}g(r,t)\right)+\frac{1}{r}\frac{\partial}{\partial r}\left( \frac{\Gamma}{2\pi r}g(r,t)\right) -\frac{1}{r^2}\frac{\Gamma}{2\pi r}g(r,t)\right)\\
\iff\    \frac{\Gamma}{2\pi r}\frac{\partial g}{\partial t} &=\nu \left(\left( 2\frac{\Gamma}{2\pi r^3}g -\frac{\Gamma}{2\pi r^2}\frac{\partial g}{\partial r} -\frac{\Gamma}{2\pi r^2}\frac{\partial g}{\partial r}+\frac{\Gamma}{2\pi r}\frac{\partial^2 g}{\partial r^2}  \right)+\frac{1}{r} \left( -\frac{\Gamma}{2\pi r^2}g +\frac{\Gamma}{2\pi r}\frac{\partial g}{\partial r} \right) -\frac{1}{r^2}\frac{\Gamma}{2\pi r}g\right)\\
    \iff\ \frac{\partial g}{\partial t} &=\nu \left(\left( \frac{2}{r^2}g -\frac{2}{r}\frac{\partial g}{\partial r} + \frac{\partial^2 g}{\partial r^2}  \right)+\frac{1}{r} \left( -\frac{1}{r}g +\frac{\partial g}{\partial r} \right) -\frac{1}{r^2}g\right)\\
    \therefore\ \frac{\partial g}{\partial t} &=\nu \left( \frac{\partial^2 g}{\partial r^2} - \frac{1}{r}\frac{\partial g}{\partial r} \right)
\end{align}
</math>
We can invoke a [[self-similar solution]], <math>g(r,t)=f(\eta)</math> with <math>\eta =r / \varphi(t) </math>, and obtain the following derivatives using the [[chain rule]]:
<math display="block"> \begin{align}
    \frac{\partial g}{\partial t} &:= \frac{\mathrm{d} f}{\mathrm{d} \eta}\frac{\partial \eta}{\partial t} = -f' \frac{r}{\varphi(t)^2}\varphi'(t)\\
    \frac{1}{r}\frac{\partial g}{\partial r}&:=\frac{1}{r}\frac{\mathrm{d} f}{\mathrm{d} \eta}\frac{\partial \eta}{\partial r} = \frac{ f'}{r\varphi(t)}\\
    \frac{\partial^2 g}{\partial r^2} &:=\frac{\partial }{\partial r}\left( \frac{\mathrm{d} f}{\mathrm{d} \eta}\frac{\partial \eta}{\partial r} \right) =\frac{\mathrm{d} f}{\mathrm{d} \eta}\underbrace{\frac{\partial}{\partial r}\left ( \frac{\partial \eta}{\partial r} \right ) }_{=0} + \frac{\partial \eta}{\partial r}\frac{\partial }{\partial r}\left ( \frac{\mathrm{d} f}{\mathrm{d} \eta} \right ) = \frac{\partial \eta}{\partial r} \cdot \frac{\mathrm{d}^2 f}{\mathrm{d} \eta^2} \frac{\partial \eta}{\partial r} = \frac{f''}{\varphi(t)^2}
\end{align} </math>
By substitution, it follows that
<math display="block">  \begin{align}    -f'\frac{r}{\varphi^2} \varphi' =\nu \left( \frac{f''}{\varphi^2} -\frac{ f'}{r\varphi} \right)\\    \iff\  f'' + \left( \eta \frac{\varphi \varphi'}{\nu}-\frac{1}{\eta} \right)f' =0 \end{align}</math>
If <math>\frac{\varphi \varphi'}{\nu}=1</math>, then <math>\varphi(t) =\sqrt{2\nu t}</math>, and hence,
<math display="block"> \begin{align}
    \frac{\mathrm{d}^2 f}{\mathrm{d}\eta^2} &= -\left( \eta -\frac{1}{\eta} \right)\frac{\mathrm{d}f}{\mathrm{d}\eta} \ \ \text{, where,} \ \ u(\eta)=f'(\eta)\\
    \iff\ \frac{\mathrm{d} u}{\mathrm{d}\eta} &= -\left( \eta-\frac{1}{\eta} \right)u \\
    \iff\ \int \frac{\mathrm{d} u}{u} &= -\int \left( \eta-\frac{1}{\eta} \right)\mathrm{d}\eta \\
    \iff\ \ln(u) &= - \left( \frac{\eta^2}{2}-\ln(\eta) \right)+C \\
    \iff\ u(\eta) &= A e^{-\frac{\eta^2}{2}+\ln(\eta)} \ \ \ \text{, where,}\ \ A= e^C \\
    \iff\ f'(\eta) &= A \eta \ e^{-\frac{\eta^2}{2}} \\
    \iff\ f(\eta) &= A \int \eta \ e^{-\frac{\eta^2}{2}} \mathrm{d}\eta \ \ \text{, where,} \ \  p=-\frac{\eta^2}{2} \ \ ,\ \ \mathrm{d}p=-\eta \ \mathrm{d}\eta \\
    \iff\ f(\eta) &= A \int \eta \left( -\frac{1}{\eta} \right)e^{p} \mathrm{d} p \\
    \iff\ f(\eta) &= -A e^{-\frac{\eta^2}{2}} +B \\
    \therefore \ g(r,t) &= B-A e^{-\frac{r^2}{4\nu t}}
\end{align} </math>
The first boundary condition, <math>v_{\theta}(0,t)=0</math>, infers that <math>g(0,t)=0</math>, which holds if and only if <math>\displaystyle \lim_{r \to 0}\frac{\Gamma}{2\pi r}g(r,t)=0</math>. Verifying by [[L'Hôpital's rule]],
<math display="block"> \begin{align}
    \displaystyle \lim_{r \to 0}\frac{\Gamma}{2\pi r}g(r,t) =\frac{\Gamma}{2\pi }\cdot \displaystyle \lim_{r \to 0}\frac{-A e^{-\frac{r^2}{4\nu t}} +B}{r} =\frac{\Gamma}{2\pi }\cdot \displaystyle \lim_{r \to 0}\frac{\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}r}\left(-A e^{-\frac{r^2}{4\nu t}}+B\right)}{\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}r}(r)} =\frac{\Gamma A}{2\pi } \cdot\displaystyle \lim_{r \to 0} \left(\frac{r}{2\nu t}e^{-\frac{r^2}{4\nu t}} \right) = 0
\end{align} </math>
The second boundary condition, <math>v_\theta (r\to \infty,t)=0</math>, is satisfied by the irrotational vortex, <math>\displaystyle \lim_{r \to \infty} \frac{\Gamma}{2\pi r}=0</math>, for all <math>t</math>. Given the third boundary condition, <math>v_\theta (r,0)=\frac{\Gamma}{2\pi r}</math>, it follows that <math>g(r,0)=B=1</math>. Likewise, <math>\forall r \in [0,\infty)</math>, the fourth boundary condition, <math>v_\theta (r,t\to \infty)=0</math>, implies that <math>\displaystyle \lim_{t \to \infty}\frac{\Gamma}{2\pi r}\left(B-A e^{-\frac{r^2}{4\nu t}} \right)=0</math>, such that <math>B=A</math>. Therefore, the solution becomes
<math display="block"> \begin{align}
    v_\theta (r,t) = \frac{\Gamma}{2\pi r}\left( 1-e^{-\frac{r^2}{4\nu t}}\right) .
\end{align} </math>
}}

{{math proof|title=Alternative derivation of the Lamb-Oseen vortex by the vorticity equation |proof=
Given the vorticity vector, <math>\boldsymbol{\omega}=\left( 0,0,\omega_z \right)</math>, the <math>z</math>-component of the linearized [[vorticity transport equation]] is <ref name="DrazinRiley" />
<math display="block"> \begin{align}
    \frac{\partial \omega_{z}}{\partial t}=\nu \left(\frac{\partial^2 \omega_{z}}{\partial r^2}+\frac{1}{r}\frac{\partial \omega_{z}}{\partial r}\right).
\end{align}</math>
If one insists on invoking the [[similarity solution]], <math>\omega_{z} (r,t)=f(\eta)</math> with <math>\eta=r/ \sqrt{2\nu t}</math> as done previously, one would exclusively obtain <math>\omega_{z}(r,t)=A \operatorname{Ei}\left( -\frac{r^2}{4\nu t}\right)+B</math> for arbitrary constants, <math>A</math> and <math>B</math>. To obtain the complete solution to <math>\omega_{z}</math>, one must introduce the [[similarity solution]], <math>\omega_{z} (r,t)=f(\eta)/t </math> with <math>\eta =r/ \sqrt{4\nu t}</math>. By the [[product rule]] and the [[chain rule]], each derivative becomes,

<math display="block"> \begin{align}
    \frac{\partial \omega_z}{\partial t} &:= \frac{\partial }{\partial t}\left(\frac{f}{t} \right)=f\frac{\partial}{\partial t}\left(\frac{1}{t}\right) +\frac{\mathrm{d} f}{\mathrm{d} \eta}\frac{\partial \eta}{\partial t} = -\frac{1}{t^2}f-\frac{2\nu r}{t(4\nu t)^{3/2}}f'\\
    \frac{1}{r}\frac{\partial \omega_z}{\partial r} &:=\frac{1}{rt}\frac{\mathrm{d} f}{\mathrm{d} \eta}\frac{\partial \eta}{\partial r} = f' \frac{1}{rt\sqrt{4\nu t}}\\
    \frac{\partial^2 \omega_z}{\partial r^2} &:=\frac{\partial }{\partial r}\left( \frac{1}{t}\frac{\mathrm{d} f}{\mathrm{d} \eta}\frac{\partial \eta}{\partial r} \right) = \frac{1}{t}\frac{\mathrm{d} f}{\mathrm{d} \eta}\underbrace{\frac{\partial}{\partial r}\left ( \frac{\partial \eta}{\partial r} \right ) }_{=0}
    + \frac{1}{t}\frac{\partial \eta}{\partial r}\frac{\partial }{\partial r}\left ( \frac{\mathrm{d} f}{\mathrm{d} \eta} \right ) = \frac{1}{t}\frac{\partial \eta}{\partial r} \cdot \frac{\mathrm{d}^2 f}{\mathrm{d} \eta^2} \frac{\partial \eta}{\partial r} = f'' \frac{1}{4\nu t^2}
\end{align} </math>
yielding the [[Sturm–Liouville]] differential equation,
<math display="block">\begin{align}
    f'' + \left(\frac{1}{\eta}+2\eta \right)f' +4f = 0.
\end{align} </math>
Because this is a differential equation of the form, 
<math display="block">\begin{align}
    y'' +f(x)y' +g(x)y &=0 \\
    \equiv\ xy'' + \frac{d}{dx}\left[ \left( xf(x)\right)y \right] &=0 \ \ \ \text{, where,} \ \ g(x)=\frac{1}{x}\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}x}\left[ xf(x) \right]
\end{align} </math>
for some function, <math>y(x)</math>, it admits the solution, <ref>{{cite book |last1=Herman |first1=Russell |title=Introduction to Partial Differential Equations |date=June 19, 2015 |publisher=R. L. Herman |pages=108-110 |url=https://people.uncw.edu/hermanr/pde1/pdebook/PDE_Main.pdf |access-date=27 June 2026 |chapter=4}}</ref>
<math display="block">\begin{align}
    y(x) &= Ce^{-\int \left[ f(x) - \frac{g(x)-f'(x)}{f(x)} \right] \mathrm{d}x}\int e^{\int \left[ f(x) - 2\frac{g(x)-f'(x)}{f(x)} \right] \mathrm{d}x} \mathrm{d}x \\
    &= Cx e^{-\int f(x) \mathrm{d}x}\int \frac{1}{x^2}e^{ \int f(x) \mathrm{d}x} \mathrm{d}x 
\end{align}</math>
This can be checked by multiplying through by <math>\eta</math> and using [[integration by parts]] as follows:
<math display="block">\begin{align}
    0 &= \eta \left( f'' + \frac{1}{\eta}f' + 2\eta f' +4f \right) \\
    \iff\ C &= \int \eta f'' d\eta + \int f' d\eta +\int 2\eta^2 f' d\eta + \int 4\eta f d\eta \\
    \iff\ C&= \left(\eta f' - \int f' d\eta \right) + \int f' d\eta  + \left(2\eta^2 f- \int 4\eta f d\eta \right) + \int 4\eta f d\eta \\
    \iff\ C&= \eta f' + 2\eta^2 f \\
    \iff\ f' + 2\eta f &= \frac{C}{\eta} \ \ \ \text{, with an integrating factor,}\ \  p(\eta)=e^{\int 2\eta d\eta}=e^{\eta^2}\\
    \iff\ e^{\eta^2}f'+ 2\eta e^{\eta^2} f &= C\frac{e^{\eta^2}}{\eta} \\
    \iff\ \frac{d}{d\eta}\left( e^{\eta^2} f\right) &= C\frac{e^{\eta^2}}{\eta} \\
    \iff\ e^{\eta^2} f &= C\int \frac{e^{\eta^2}}{\eta}d\eta \\
    \therefore\ f(\eta) &= C \operatorname{Ei}(\eta^2)e^{-\eta^2} +C_1e^{-\eta^2} 
\end{align}</math>
Because <math>\displaystyle \lim_{\eta\to 0} \operatorname{Ei}(\eta^2)</math> is not well defined, <math>C=0</math>. Substituting <math>\eta</math> and <math>f(\eta)</math> into <math>\omega_{z} (r,t)=f(\eta)/t</math> yields,
<math display="block">\begin{align}
    \omega_z (r,t)= \frac{C_1}{t}e^{-\frac{r^2}{4\nu t}}
\end{align}</math>
The [[Circulation (fluid dynamics)| circulation flux integral]] over a surface, <math>S =\left\{ (r,\theta)\in \mathbb{R}^2 \ | \ 0\leq r \leq \infty  ,\ 0\leq \theta \leq 2\pi \right\}</math>, may be solved for constant circulation, <math>\Gamma</math>.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Gottlieb |first1=Michael |last2=Pfeiffer |first2=Rudolf |last3=Leighton |first3=Ralph |title=The Feynman Lectures on Physics Vol. II Ch. 17: The Laws of Induction |url=https://www.feynmanlectures.caltech.edu/II_03.html |publisher=California Institute of Technology |access-date=28 June 2026}}</ref>
<math display="block">\begin{align}
    \Gamma := \iint_{S} \boldsymbol{\omega} \cdot \mathrm{d}\boldsymbol{S} &= \int_{0}^{2\pi}\int_{0}^{\infty} \omega_z \cdot r\mathrm{d}r \mathrm{d}\theta\\ 
    &= 2\pi\int_{0}^{\infty} \frac{C_1}{t}e^{-\frac{r^2}{4\nu t}} \cdot r \mathrm{d}r \\
    &= 4\pi \nu C_1 \int_{0}^{\infty} e^{-u}  \mathrm{d}u  \ \ \ \text{where,} \ \ \ u=\frac{r^2}{4\nu t} \\
    \therefore C_1 &= \frac{\Gamma}{4\pi \nu }.
\end{align}</math>
Since,
<math display="block"> \omega_{z} = \frac{\partial v_\theta}{\partial r}+\frac{v_\theta}{r} -\frac{1}{r}\frac{\partial v_r}{\partial \theta}</math> 
bearing in mind that <math> v_r =0</math>, we can use the integrating factor, <math>e^{\int \frac{1}{r} dr}=r</math>, to isolate <math>v_\theta</math>.
<math display="block">\begin{align}
    v_\theta (r,t) &= \frac{1}{r}\int r\omega_{z} \mathrm{d}r \\
    &= \frac{\Gamma}{4\pi \nu t} \frac{1}{r}\int r e^{-\frac{r^2}{4\nu t}} \mathrm{d}r \\
    &= \frac{\Gamma}{4\pi \nu t} \frac{1}{r}\int r e^{u} \left(-\frac{2\nu t}{r} \right) \mathrm{d}u \ \ \ \text{, where,}\ \  u=-\frac{r^2}{4\nu t} \\
    &= \frac{\Gamma}{2\pi r} \left(C_2-e^{-\frac{r^2}{4\nu t}} \right) \\
\end{align}</math>
The aforementioned boundary conditions on <math>v_\theta</math> yields the Lamb-Oseen vortex.
}}

== Generalized Oseen vortex ==
The generalized Oseen vortex may be obtained by looking for solutions of the form
: <math>v_r=-\gamma(t) r, \quad v_\theta= \frac{\Gamma}{2\pi r}g(r,t), \quad v_z = 2\gamma(t) z</math>
that leads to the equation
: <math>\frac{\partial g}{\partial t} -\gamma r\frac{\partial g}{\partial r} = \nu \left(\frac{\partial^2 g}{\partial r^2} - \frac{1}{r} \frac{\partial g}{\partial r}\right).</math>

[[Self-similar solution]] exists for the coordinate {{tmath|1= \eta=r/\varphi(t) }}, provided {{tmath|1= \varphi\varphi' +\gamma \varphi^2=a }}, where <math>a</math> is a constant, in which case {{tmath|1= g=1-\mathrm{e}^{-a\eta^2/2\nu} }}. The solution for <math>\varphi(t)</math> may be written according to Rott (1958)<ref>Rott, N. (1958). On the viscous core of a line vortex. Zeitschrift für angewandte Mathematik und Physik ZAMP, 9(5-6), 543–553.</ref> as
: <math>\varphi^2= 2a\exp\left(-2\int_0^t\gamma(s)\,\mathrm{d} s\right)\int_c^t\exp\left(2\int_0^u \gamma(s)\,\mathrm{d} s\right)\,\mathrm{d}u,</math>
where <math>c</math> is an arbitrary constant. For {{tmath|1= \gamma=0 }}, the classical Lamb–Oseen vortex is recovered. The case <math>\gamma=k</math> corresponds to the axisymmetric [[stagnation point flow]], where <math>k</math> is a constant. When {{tmath|1= c=-\infty }}, {{tmath|1= \varphi^2=a/k }}, a [[Burgers vortex]] is a obtained. For arbitrary {{tmath| c }}, the solution becomes {{tmath|1= \varphi^2=a(1+\beta \mathrm{e}^{-2kt})/k }}, where <math>\beta</math> is an arbitrary constant. As {{tmath| t\rightarrow\infty }}, Burgers vortex is recovered.
